summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands and stands under that national framework; the island's own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions that apply here. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only. Gender identity and gender expression are not addressed anywhere in the provision, so a trans visitor has no statutory ground of protection against discrimination in Aruba.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.

Relationship recognition has moved in steps. On 8 September 2016 the Staten of Aruba voted 11 to 5, with four abstentions, to extend the civil code's marriage articles to registered unions open to same-sex couples, granting spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must also recognise same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore enters a jurisdiction where such marriages and unions are recognised, while gender identity itself remains outside the discrimination statute.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation at that endorsement acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatised as disordered.

Documented harassment is on the record. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge of 2004 to 2007, which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognise same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition. The most recent documented instance of such harassment in this record is from 2007; no later instance is documented.

The official Aruba tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling safe, secure and welcome as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. That is the destination's own marketer speaking rather than independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

Several gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly.
tangentialFactors:
Associated Press reporting of 9 September 2016 recorded that religious and cultural opposition to the registered-union measure was strong, and that neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions at the time. Aruba's own news service reported the vote as making the island the first in the Caribbean to act, a claim about order of enactment rather than a measure of risk.

The campaign behind the 2016 vote ran 2.5 years, was sponsored by openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes, and carried an Igualdad Aruba petition of nearly 20,000 signatures. The Associated Press noted that marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised throughout the Kingdom and that the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route.

GlobalGayz, a cultural report edited in January 2017, describes Aruba as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curaçao, and identifies Catholic influence as the main brake on further change. The same report notes that the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands.

The Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba is quoted as saying: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.' The formulation describes a local norm of low visibility rather than a legal guarantee, and it is a community organisation's own characterisation.
localsOnly:
Residents' registered unions, opened by the 8 September 2016 amendment, carry spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights, and same-sex adoption is legal. Because the Criminal Code's enumerated grounds stop at sexual orientation, residents have no statutory discrimination claim founded on gender identity or gender expression.

Several LGBT associations operate on the island, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. Openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes publicly introduced the registered partnership bill in August 2016.

Aruba's representation at the 22 April 2015 Kingdom endorsement acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatised as disordered. That acknowledgement is an official statement about local conditions for young people, not a visitor-facing rule.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific violence or killing figure for Aruba appears in this inventory, and no general homicide rate is available for comparison, so no trans-specific rate can be stated or ranked.

Nothing is sourced on gender-marker rules for passports or identity documents, on entry or visa screening, or on how border and security officials treat binders, packers, prosthetics or gender presentation at Queen Beatrix International or at any other port of entry. Whether document-marker flagging or targeted inspection occurs is unresolved here.

Also unsourced: enforcement practice under Articles 2:61 and 2:62, any case law on gender-identity discrimination, gender-affirming healthcare access, facility and restroom rules, and custody treatment. Whether the 12 July 2024 marriage ruling or the 2016 registered-union regime addresses a marriage involving a trans person is not stated in any source.

The tourism board page and the GlobalGayz report are self-description and cultural reporting, not independent evidence of treatment. The harassment record in this inventory ends in 2007, and no later instance is documented; the absence of later documentation does not establish that such incidents have ended.
